questions.learningObjective: Identify the formula for radius of curvature
questions.stem: Which expression gives radius of curvature from speed and centripetal acceleration?

options.text: Speed divided by centripetal acceleration
Centripetal acceleration divided by speed squared
Speed squared divided by centripetal acceleration
Speed times centripetal acceleration

questions.explanation: From a = v^2/r, radius r = v^2/a. Speed is squared and divided by acceleration.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_MECHANICS
questions.topic: Time for one full revolution
questions.learningObjective: Identify the formula for period
questions.stem: Which expression gives the period of circular motion from radius and speed?

options.text: Radius divided by speed, omitting 2π
Speed divided by 2π times radius
2π times speed divided by radius
2π times radius divided by speed

questions.explanation: Period T = circumference/speed = 2πr/v. Circumference is 2πr.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_MECHANICS
questions.topic: Centripetal acceleration at the top of a wheel
questions.learningObjective: Compute acceleration for new values
questions.stem: A wheel point moves at 14 m/s around a 7 m radius; what centripetal acceleration in m/s^2 at the top?
questions.explanation: a = v^2/r = 196/7 = 28 m/s^2 toward the center. Position does not change magnitude.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_MECHANICS
questions.topic: Centripetal acceleration scales with radius
questions.learningObjective: Compute acceleration for doubled radius
questions.stem: A bee flies at 8 m/s on a 4 m radius, then on an 8 m radius; what is the new acceleration in m/s^2?
questions.explanation: a = v^2/r = 64/8 = 8 m/s^2. Doubling radius halves acceleration from 16 to 8.
questions.hint: Square speed, divide by new radius.

questions.topic: Normal force direction on a bank
questions.learningObjective: Analyze a claim about normal force direction
questions.stem: A log note says the normal force on a banked curve points straight up; find the error.

options.text: The note is correct
Normal force is perpendicular to the surface, so it tilts inward
Normal force points along the surface
Normal force points horizontally inward only

questions.explanation: The normal force is perpendicular to the banked surface, not vertical. It has both vertical and inward horizontal components.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_MECHANICS
questions.topic: Cornering speed with no friction needed
questions.learningObjective: Explain the effect of radius on design speed
questions.stem: Explain why a larger radius banked curve has a higher frictionless design speed.

answer.exemplar: Since design speed v equals square root of r g tan theta, a larger radius r increases the value under the square root, raising the speed at which the normal force's horizontal component suffices.

questions.explanation: Design speed grows with the square root of radius. Larger radius means gentler curvature and higher allowable speed.
questions.hint: Design speed scales with square root of radius.

questions.topic: Angular speed from a tangential speed
questions.learningObjective: Compute angular speed for new values
questions.stem: A bee flies at 15 m/s around a 5 m radius; what angular speed in rad/s is logged?
questions.explanation: ω = v/r = 15/5 = 3 rad/s. Angular speed is tangential speed divided by radius.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_MECHANICS
questions.topic: Radius from a period and a tangential speed
questions.learningObjective: Compute radius for new values
questions.stem: A bee completes one revolution in 8 s at 6 m/s; what radius in meters?
questions.explanation: r = vT/(2π) = 6*8/(2π) = 7.64 m. Longer period or higher speed increases radius.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_MECHANICS
questions.topic: Centripetal acceleration scales with radius
questions.learningObjective: Explain inverse radius dependence
questions.stem: Explain why halving the radius at fixed speed doubles the centripetal acceleration.

answer.exemplar: Centripetal acceleration equals v squared divided by r, so halving r doubles the denominator's reciprocal, doubling acceleration while speed stays the same.

questions.explanation: Acceleration is inversely proportional to radius. Halving radius doubles acceleration at fixed speed.
questions.hint: Acceleration is inversely proportional to radius.
